items.title: The two lost children
items.author: Tim Keller
items.work: The Prodigal God (2008)
items.body:
Almost everyone knows the parable of the prodigal son: the young man who asks for the inheritance, wastes everything far from home, and returns ashamed, being welcomed with a party by his father. Tim Keller, a pastor in New York for almost thirty years, drew attention to a detail that often goes unnoticed: the story of Luke 15 has two sons, and the second ends outside the party.

## Two paths away from God

The younger son represents the path of self-discovery: "my life, my rules." The older represents the path of moral self-affirmation: he obeys, works, never disrespects his father. Keller observes that the two, by opposite paths, want the same thing: the father's wealth, not the father himself. One breaks the rules to get what he wants; the other keeps the rules so that the father owes him something.

Therefore, when grace appears, the older brother becomes furious. The feast for the repentant sinner reveals that his obedience was a contract, not love. Jesus told the parable precisely to the Pharisees and scribes, religious and upright people, who murmured because he ate with sinners.

## The true older brother

The most beautiful point of the book is the question: where, in this story, is the older brother who should have gone to get the youngest? Keller answers that Jesus is the true older brother. He did not wait in the field; he left the Father's house, went to the distant land, and paid with his own life the cost of our return. The inheritance that the youngest wasted, Christ returns at his expense.

## What does this change today

Keller insists that the gospel is neither religion nor irreligion, but a third thing. We are not accepted because we obey; we obey because we have already been accepted. This humiliates the moralist and lifts up the defeated at the same time. The question is worth asking the heart: in what way am I more like the eldest son? Where is my obedience a way of demanding from God?

The door of the celebration remains open for the two children. The invitation is to enter, not by one's own merits, but by the love of the Father and the work of the Brother who came to fetch us.

items.title: Children of God: the greatest privilege of the gospel
items.author: J. I. Packer
items.work: Knowing God (1973)
items.body:
In The Knowledge of God, one of the most widely read Christian books of the twentieth century, the Anglican and Reformed theologian J. I. Packer asks a simple question: how can we summarize the New Testament in a few words? His answer is surprising: Christianity boils down to the knowledge of God as Father, through Jesus Christ.

## More than forgiveness

Packer explains that justification, being declared righteous before God by faith in Christ, is the fundamental blessing of the gospel. Without it, nothing else exists. But adoption is the highest privilege. A judge can acquit a defendant and send him away; a father brings the child into the house. In justification, God is the judge who acquits us; in adoption, He is the Father who embraces us, gives us His name, and makes us heirs.

## How a child lives

For Packer, adoption explains the entire Christian life. Holiness becomes the likeness of family: the child wants to resemble the father. Prayer ceases to be a formality and becomes a household conversation, as Jesus taught: "Our Father." Security comes from the Father's character, not from our performance, because a father does not expel the son with every failure. And even discipline takes on another meaning: God corrects those He loves, as Hebrews 12 says.

## The Spirit that cries out "Aba"

The apostle Paul says that we receive the Spirit of adoption, through whom we cry out "Abba, Father" (Romans 8:15). Packer reminds us that this certainty is not the result of psychological effort; it is the work of the Holy Spirit, who testifies with our spirit that we are children of God.

## To take with you

Packer proposes a practical test: how much do you think of yourself as a child of God? If the answer is "little," perhaps your faith is working more as a contract than as a family. The gospel invites us to wake up every morning knowing who we are: beloved children, called by name, with a Father who does not abandon His.

items.title: All for grace
items.author: Charles H. Spurgeon
items.work: All of Grace (1886)
items.body:
Charles Spurgeon, the "prince of preachers," preached to crowds in London in the nineteenth century. Among dozens of books, he wrote a small volume intended for those who were not yet Christians or had doubts about their own salvation. The title sums up the message: all by grace.

## God justifies the wicked

Spurgeon begins with Romans 4:5: God justifies the wicked. He notes that many people think the gospel is for the good, and that it needs to be improved before it comes to God. But the Bible says otherwise. Christ came to save sinners. No one is too good to need grace, and no one is too bad to receive it.

## Grace through faith

Spurgeon explains faith with simple images. Faith is like the hand that receives a gift, or like the pipe through which water arrives. Value is not in the pipe, but in the source. We are not saved because our faith is strong, but because the Christ we believe in is strong. A small faith in a great Savior saves completely.

## What if I fall again?

Part of the book deals with the fear of not persevering. Spurgeon answers that the one who started the work is God Himself, and He does not abandon what He begun. The grace that called us also guards us. This is not permission to sin, because those who have been reached by grace begin to hate sin and love those who saved them.

## A direct invitation

The book ends with a personal appeal, typical of Spurgeon: do not delay. He writes to the reader as if speaking face to face: look to Christ now. Do not expect to feel something special or become worthy. The door is open to you today.

items.title: God's Elect: the sovereignty that saves us
items.author: R. C. Sproul
items.work: Chosen by God (1986)
items.body:
R. C. Sproul, founder of the Ligonier ministry, confessed that he resisted the doctrine of predestination for years. He accepted it, he says, not because he found it comfortable, but because he could not escape it in the Scriptures. The book God's Elect was born from this struggle and became one of the clearest introductions to the subject.

## The problem is not God, it is us

Sproul begins with the point that weighs most: the human condition. The Bible says we were dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1). A dead person does not cooperate with their own resurrection. If God only offered salvation and waited for our initiative, no one would come, because a fallen heart does not want God. Election, therefore, is not an obstacle to salvation; it is the only reason someone is saved.

## Justice and mercy

The most common objection is: "That is unjust." Sproul responds by distinguishing justice from mercy. No one receives injustice from God. Some receive justice, others receive mercy, which by definition is not due. The Christian's astonishment should not be "why didn't God choose everyone?", but "why would He choose me?".

## Doctrine to worship, not to discuss

For Sproul, God's sovereignty in salvation produces three fruits. Humility, because there is nothing to boast about. Security, because what God has begun He will complete (Philippians 1:6). And missionary courage, because God has a people in every nation, and the gospel proclaimed will be the means by which He will call Him.

## A pastoral word

No one needs to decipher God's eternal decree to rest in it. The right question is not "was I elected?", but "am I trusting in Christ?". Whoever comes to Christ discovers that they were brought by the Father (John 6:37 and 44). The doctrine of election does not close the door; it explains why the door was opened.

items.title: The providence that consoles us
items.author: João Calvino
items.work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book I, chapters 16–17 (1559)
items.body:
John Calvin wrote about God's providence not as a cold philosopher, but as a refugee pastor. Geneva was full of people who had lost home, family, and country because of faith. For them, the question "who rules the world?" was not theoretical.

## Nothing happens by chance

In the Institutes, Calvin rejects the idea that God created the world and left it functioning alone, like a watchmaker who strays from the work. He also rejects fate and blind destiny. God governs all things, from great to small: not a sparrow falls without the will of the Father (Matthew 10:29). But Calvin insists that God governs as Father, not as an impersonal force.

## Three consoles

The reformer draws three practical fruits from this doctrine. First, gratitude in good things: every blessing comes from God's hand, not just from our own competence. Second, patience in difficult things: adversity is also under the governance of a wise Father, who uses it for our good (Romans 8:28). Third, freedom regarding the future: whoever knows that tomorrow is in God's hands can work diligently without being crushed by anxiety.

## Providence is not fatalism

Calvin warns against two errors. One is to use providence as an excuse for laziness: God governs by means, and prudence, work, and remedy are part of those means. The other is blaming God for the evil we do: human responsibility remains real. Providence does not nullify our action; it involves it.

## For today

Calvin's question remains relevant: when life gets out of control, do you think of chance or of Father? The Heidelberg Catechism, heir to this tradition, sums up the consolation as follows: nothing can separate us from God's love, because all creatures are so in His hands that, without His will, they cannot even move.

items.title: All things cooperate for good
items.author: Thomas Watson
items.work: All Things Work Together for Good (A Divine Cordial, 1663)
items.body:
Thomas Watson was an English Puritan pastor expelled from the pulpit in 1662, along with about two thousand ministers who did not accept the impositions of the official Church. The following year, he published an entire book about a single verse: "we know that all things work together for the good of those who love God" (Romans 8:28). Watson wrote about providence while living the loss of his ministry.

## Good things cooperate

Watson starts with the easiest: God's attributes, promises, mercies, prayers of the saints, and even angels work for the good of the believer. Everything that comes from God is for us.

## The bad things too

Then comes the most difficult and consoling point. Afflictions, temptations, desertions, and even our sins, while still evil, are used by God for our good. Affliction humbles us and teaches us to pray. Temptation makes us depend on Christ. The fall, when it generates repentance, makes us more vigilant and more grateful for grace. God does not approve of evil, but governs it.

## Who is the promise for

Watson insists on a condition of the verse: to those who love God. The promise is not for everyone indiscriminately, but for those who have been called and love God. That is why he devotes pages to examining whether we truly love God: whether we think of Him with pleasure, whether we hate what He hates, whether we desire His presence.

## A cordial to the heart

The original title speaks of a cordial, a remedy that strengthens the heart. Watson wanted the believer to take this truth as a daily remedy. When life seems messy, he invites us to remember: the God who governs all things is working for my good, even when I still don't see how.

items.title: Prayer: conversation and encounter
items.author: Tim Keller
items.work: Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God, 2014)
items.body:
Tim Keller confesses that, even after years as a pastor, his prayer life was weak. A family illness and a personal crisis led him to seek God in another way, and from that search the book Prayer was born. The thesis is simple: prayer is at once conversation and encounter, duty and pleasure, wonder and intimacy.

## Answering God who spoke first

Keller reminds us that Christian prayer does not begin within us. God spoke first, in His Word, and prayer is our response. That is why he recommends combining biblical reading and prayer: reading a passage, meditating on it, and then transforming what was read into praise, confession, and request. The Psalms are the great school of this practice.

## Learning from the masters

The book dialogues with Augustine, Luther, and Calvin. From Luther, Keller takes the habit of praying from the Our Father, phrase by phrase, paraphrasing each request with its own needs. From Calvin, the idea that true prayer has reverence, dependence, humility, and trust. From Augustine, the certainty that, deep down, we ask God to give us Himself.

## Astonishment and intimacy

Keller observes that many people have only one side. Some approach God with reverence but without warmth. Others have intimacy but have lost fear. In the gospel, the two meet: the holy God is also the Father who receives us in Christ. Mature prayer combines worship before God's greatness and rest before His love.

## A practical step

Keller suggests starting with the simple: two moments a day, morning and evening, with a short reading, a few minutes of meditation, and free prayer. Don't expect to feel the urge to pray; pray until you feel it. Prayer is, as he says, the main way to truly experience what we believe.

items.title: Prayer is a war radio
items.author: John Piper
items.work: Let the Nations Be Glad! (Let the Nations Be Glad!, 1993)
items.body:
John Piper, a pastor for more than three decades in Minneapolis and founder of the Desiring God ministry, uses a striking image to talk about prayer. Many Christians, he says, treat prayer as a home intercom: a device to ask for comfort, another pillow, a little more convenience. But prayer was given for times of war.

## The campaign radio

In Piper's image, the Christian life is a mission in hostile territory. The commander sent his soldiers with a task and gave them a radio to ask for reinforcements whenever needed. Jesus said: "Whatever you ask in my name, I will do" (John 14:13), precisely in the context of sending the disciples to bear fruit. Prayer is the church's campaign radio on mission.

## Why prayer weakens

When we forget we are at war, prayer loses its meaning. If life is just comfort, radio seems unnecessary. Piper notes that the weakness of prayer often reveals a life without mission. Anyone trying to reach a neighbor, raise children in faith, or serve in the church quickly discovers they need help from above.

## God receives the glory

For Piper, prayer exists so that God may be glorified as the giver. The one who asks acknowledges that they cannot; the one who receives gives thanks to those who can. This is the logic of all his theology: God is most glorified in us when we are most satisfied in Him. In prayer, our need and the glory of God go hand in hand.

## To pray today

Piper suggests a concrete practice: plan prayer as one plans anything important. Mark time, place, and a list of mission-related requests: people to reach, church ministries, missionaries, nations. And ask boldly, because the radio was delivered by a commander who wants to win.

items.title: Prayer and revival
items.author: Hernandes Dias Lopes
items.work: Recurring theme in his books, expository commentaries, and sermons
items.body:
Hernandes Dias Lopes is a Presbyterian pastor in Brazil, known throughout the country for his sermons and expository commentaries on books of the Bible. One theme frequently appears in his ministry: the relationship between prayer and revival. This article presents, in our own words, the core of this emphasis.

## The church is born by praying

Hernandes often recalls that the church in Acts was born in a prayer meeting. Before Pentecost, the disciples persevered unanimously in prayer (Acts 1:14). Before boldness in preaching, there was a cry that made the place where they were tremble (Acts 4:31). In reading it, the church's history shows the same pattern: God acts when His people humble themselves and pray.

## Revival is not an event

An important distinction in Reformed preaching on the subject is that revival is not a restless service nor a campaign marked on the calendar. It is a sovereign visitation from God that leads the church to repentance, love for the Word, holiness, and care for the lost. It is not fabricated; it is asked. That is why prayer is the way, and the Word is the content.

## Word and prayer together

Hernandes insists that prayer without the Word becomes mysticism, and the Word without prayer becomes cold intellectualism. The apostles said: "we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word" (Acts 6:4). Preachers and churches need both to see lives transformed.

## A call for today

The practical challenge is to start with your own heart: set aside daily prayer time, pray for your church and pastors, and participate in community prayer meetings. The revival we desire for the church begins with the breaking we allow within us.

items.title: Kill the sin, or it will kill you
items.author: John Owen
items.work: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656)
items.body:
John Owen, the great English Puritan theologian, preached to young Oxford students a series of sermons on Romans 8:13: "if, by the Spirit, you put to death the works of the body, you will surely live." From these sermons was born a small book that, more than three centuries later, remains one of the most serious guides on the fight against sin.

## A lifelong struggle

The most remembered phrase from the work sums up urgency: always kill sin, or it will kill you. Owen teaches that the sin that remains in the believer does not take a vacation. He is not satisfied with little; he always wants to go to the extreme. That is why mortification is not a one-time event, but a daily habit.

## What mortification is not

Owen makes valuable distinctions. Mortifying is not just hiding sin or exchanging one vice for another. It is not simply calming the conscience after a fall. And it is not the work of willpower: only the Holy Spirit kills sin. Purely human attempts, Owen says, produce pride or despair, never holiness.

## How to fight

The path Owen proposes involves concrete steps: honestly considering the gravity of sin without diminishing it; filling the conscience with the guilt it brings; ardently desiring deliverance; watching for the occasions that feed it; and, above all, looking to Christ. Faith that contemplates Christ crucified weakens sin at its root because it fills the heart with greater love.

## Hope in combat

The book is not dark. Owen writes for believers who are already united to Christ, to whom the final victory is guaranteed. The struggle is real, but it is the struggle of those who have already been set free. Every small victory, by the Spirit, is a sign of life. And every fall is a reason to run again to Christ, not away from Him.

items.title: The root and the fruit: how people change
items.author: Paul David Tripp
items.work: Instruments in the Hands of the Redeemer (2002) and How People Change (with Timothy Lane)
items.body:
Paul David Tripp, pastor and Bible counselor, spent his life helping people change. One idea runs through his books: behavior is fruit, and fruit reveals the root. If we want true change, we need to go beyond what people do and reach what they love.

## The heart as the center of control

Tripp uses the biblical image of the tree (Luke 6:43–45). A bad tree does not bear good fruit, no matter how much apples are glued to the branches. Likewise, rules and techniques may restrain behavior for a time, but they do not transform the person. The Bible calls the heart the center from which our desires, thoughts, and choices flow, and it is there that God works.

## Idols of the heart

Behind anger, anxiety, or addiction, Tripp almost always finds a desire that has grown too much: approval, control, comfort, success. Good things that have become supreme things. When that desire is countered, the heart reacts with sin. Questions like "what did I want at that moment?" and "what did I fear losing?" help to see the root.

## Heat, thorns, cross, and fruit

In How People Change, Tripp and Timothy Lane describe the process with four images. The heat is the difficult circumstances. The thorns are our sinful reactions. The cross is Christ, who forgives us and gives us a new heart. And the fruit is the new response, generated by grace, in the same circumstances. Change does not come from changing the heat, but from finding Christ in its midst.

## To apply

Tripp reminds us that we are all instruments in the hands of the Redeemer. He wants to use ordinary people—parents, friends, and church brothers—to help others see their own heart with love and hope. The question is not just "how do I change?" but also "how can I be God's tool in someone's life today?"

items.title: Holiness, without which no one will see the Lord
items.author: J. C. Ryle
items.work: Holiness (Holiness, 1877)
items.body:
J. C. Ryle was the first Anglican bishop of Liverpool and one of the most widely read evangelical writers in Victorian England. In his time, teachings were growing promising instant holiness, achieved by a step of faith, without struggle. Ryle responded with a clear and firm book, based on Hebrews 12:14: "I have pursued holiness, without which no one will see the Lord."

## Holiness is fruit, not root

Ryle begins with sin. No one understands holiness without understanding how deep sin is. Then he distinguishes: we are justified only by faith, and sanctification is the inevitable fruit of that justification. Those who have truly been forgiven begin to be transformed. A faith that does not produce holiness is not the faith that saves.

## A real struggle

The best-known chapter deals with struggle. Ryle says that the true Christian is a soldier. He fights the world, the flesh, and the devil every day. Peace with God brings war with sin. That is why he distrusts those who say they live without inner conflict. Struggle is not a sign of defeat; it is a sign of life.

## Marks of a holy person

Ryle describes practical traits: the holy person seeks to please God in everything, hates sin, follows Christ's example, grows in humility, meekness, and self-control, cares for others, and loves the Word and prayer. He warns that no one has all these marks perfectly, but the course of life points in that direction.

## A sincere appeal

Ryle didn't want to scare but to awaken. He asks the reader: are you growing in holiness? Not to conquer heaven, but because whoever goes to heaven already begins to resemble him here. The path is to look to Christ, use the means of grace, and persevere.

items.title: The meaning of marriage
items.author: Tim Keller (com Kathy Keller)
items.work: The Meaning of Marriage (2011)
items.body:
Tim Keller wrote The Meaning of Marriage with his wife, Kathy, based on more than thirty-five years of living together and many sermons on Ephesians 5. The book speaks to both married and single people, and begins by dispelling a common illusion: that the ideal marriage is to find someone perfectly compatible.

## No one is compatible

The Kellers remember that every marriage unites two sinners. Over time, each discovers that the other is more selfish than it seemed. And, worse, discovers selfishness itself. The question is not whether there will be conflict, but what to do when it comes. The answer is in the gospel: Christ loved the church when it was not yet lovable, and gave Himself for it.

## Covenant, not just feeling

The biblical marriage is a covenant: a public promise that sustains love on days when feeling fails. The Kellers say that promise does not imprison love; it protects it. Loving is often a decision to act kindly before feeling returns.

## Spiritual friendship

One of the most beautiful chapters describes marriage as friendship with a common destiny. Husband and wife are companions on the journey toward whom God wants each to be. Each spouse sees in the other the future "glorious self" that God is forming and works to help them get there, with truth and love.

## For married and single people

The book reminds us that marriage is not the ultimate fulfillment of life. It points to something greater: Christ's marriage to His church. Therefore, singles are not incomplete Christians, and married people should not expect their spouse to be a god. Only Christ can satisfy the heart; and whoever is satisfied in Him is free to truly love the other.

items.title: What did you expect? Marriage between sinners
items.author: Paul David Tripp
items.work: What Did You Expect? (2010)
items.body:
Paul Tripp opens his book on marriage with a confession: after years of marriage, he realized that he and his wife, Luella, were trapped in a cycle of irritation. There was no major scandal, only small accumulated insults. He concludes that most marriages don't die all at once; they die from small negligences.

## Realistic expectations

The title asks: what did you expect? Tripp says we enter marriage with unrealistic expectations about the other and about ourselves. We forget that we are sinners, that we live in a fallen world, and that God is more interested in our holiness than in our comfort. When reality arrives, disappointment turns into demand.

## Six commitments

Tripp proposes daily commitments that keep the marriage healthy. Confess and forgive quickly, without letting the offense sleep. Build a love that is stronger than resentment. Deal with differences with grace, not with attempts to turn the other into a copy of yourself. Make trust something that is rebuilt through small fidelities. Cultivate love like a garden, with constant care. And remember that worship comes before everything else: whoever worships God does not need their spouse to be their god.

## Grace for everyday life

The central theme is that God's grace is not only for conversion; it is for Monday morning, for traffic, for the overdue bill, for the harsh word in the kitchen. Marriage transforms when each one approaches the other as someone who also needs grace.

## A question for today

Tripp suggests asking: what little neglect have I allowed in my marriage? What word of forgiveness am I putting off? The path to a better marriage rarely begins with big gestures; it starts with small decisions of fidelity.

items.title: The Christian family
items.author: Herman Bavinck
items.work: The Christian Family (Het christelijk huisgezin, 1908)
items.body:
Herman Bavinck, a Dutch Reformed theologian, is best known for his great Reformed Dogmatics. But he also wrote for the common church. In 1908, he published a book about the family, at a time when modernity was beginning to question marriage and the home. His reflections remain relevant today.

## Family comes from God

Bavinck begins with creation. The family is not a social invention nor a contract that we can redraw at will; it was instituted by God in Eden. Marriage between man and woman, the generation of children, and communal life are part of the Creator's design for the world. That is why the family has its own dignity.

## Wounded by sin, restored by grace

Bavinck does not idealize the family. He shows how sin has struck the home since Genesis 3: domination, conflict, jealousy, violence. But the grace of Christ does not destroy the family; it heals and elevates it. The gospel transforms husbands, wives, fathers, and children from the inside out.

## The school of love

A beautiful idea in the book is that the family is humanity's first school. There we learn authority and obedience, care and responsibility, forgiveness and patience. Bavinck said that the whole society depends on the health of homes. When the family falls apart, the whole community suffers.

## For today

Bavinck reminds us that the family is important, but it is not God. It serves the Kingdom and points to God's greater family, the church. That is why a Christian home should be a place of worship, hospitality, and service, where faith is lived and passed on, from generation to generation.

items.title: Shepherding the child's heart
items.author: Tedd Tripp
items.work: Shepherding a Child's Heart (1995)
items.body:
Tedd Tripp, pastor and brother of Paul Tripp, wrote one of the most influential books on raising children in the Reformed environment. The thesis starts from Proverbs 4:23: "Over everything that must be kept, keep your heart, for out of it proceed the sources of life." Educating children is not just about correcting behaviors; it is about shepherding hearts.

## Behind the behavior

Tripp notes that the child who hits his brother to get a toy does not just have a behavioral problem. He has a heart that desires something more than he wants to love his neighbor. If parents only deal with behavior, they teach the child to hide the heart. If they treat the heart, they lead them to realize their need for Christ.

## Influences that shape

The book distinguishes the influences that shape the child (family, school, friends, culture) from the orientation of the heart itself toward God. Parents do not control this orientation, but are called to be faithful instruments. This removes from parents the illusion of omnipotence and, at the same time, calls them to responsibility.

## Communication and correction

Tripp advocates for rich communication: talking, listening, asking, teaching with the Scriptures, and not just giving orders. Correction exists, but always with the goal of restoring and pointing to the cross. The child needs to hear that the father and mother also sin and also need the same Savior.

## The gospel at home

The ultimate goal is not to have well-behaved children, but children who know grace. When parents ask forgiveness from their children, pray with them, and show that Christ is the hope of the family, the home becomes the first place where the gospel is seen and not just heard.

items.title: Parents as ambassadors of God
items.author: Paul David Tripp
items.work: Parenting: 14 Gospel Principles (2016)
items.body:
In the book Parenting, Paul Tripp proposes that parents change the question they ask themselves. Instead of "how do I produce good children?", the question should be "how can I be an instrument of God in their lives?". For Tripp, parents are ambassadors: they represent a King, carry his message, and do not act on their own behalf.

## Called, not controlled

Many parents, says Tripp, live tired and frustrated because they try to do what only God can do: change their children's hearts. When they take on the role of ambassadors, they are free to do what is their duty, faithfully, and entrust God with the outcome.

## The small moments

Tripp insists that raising children happens in ordinary moments: the car fight, homework, the lie discovered, the disappointment with a friend. These moments are opportunities God places before parents to show who He is. An angry father sees interruption; an ambassador sees opportunity.

## Law and grace

Children need law: clear boundaries, authority, consequences. But Tripp reminds us that the law shows sin and has no power to heal it. Only grace changes hearts. That is why parents must apply rules without losing their tone of grace, pointing to Christ, who fulfilled the law for us.

## Parents' identity

Another important principle: parents should not seek their identity in their children. When the success of children becomes the source of value for parents, the house becomes heavy. Those who rest in Christ can love their children without needing them to be perfect.

items.title: The path the child should walk
items.author: J. C. Ryle
items.work: The Duties of Parents (1888)
items.body:
J. C. Ryle wrote a short and very practical sermon on Proverbs 22:6: "teach the child the way he ought to walk, and even when he is old, he will not turn away from it." The text became a small book, still read today by Christian parents. Ryle lists direct advice, almost like a manual.

## Educating on the right path

Ryle begins by reminding that a child should be educated on the path they should walk, not the path they would like to follow. The child's heart, like all of ours, tends toward sin. That's why parents can't simply let them follow their own desires. To love is to guide.

## Practical advice

Among Ryle's advice are: educate with tenderness and patience, not harshness; teach the Bible early and regularly; teach the child to pray; take them to services and explain what happens there; teach obedience and truthfulness; take care of company and influences; and remember that parental example teaches more than words. He insists that parents should not postpone it, because childhood passes quickly.

## The parents' prayer

Ryle ends with the most important advice: pray for your children. Parents can plant and water, but only God gives growth. No technique replaces grace. That is why Christian parents educate diligently and pray with dependence.

## To take with you

Ryle does not promise automatic results. Proverbs teaches principles of wisdom, not mechanical guarantees. But he encourages parents to trust in God, who often blesses faithfulness. The practical question is: what concrete step can I take this week to teach the Word to my children?

items.title: Stop listening to yourself and start talking to yourself
items.author: Martyn Lloyd-Jones
items.work: Spiritual Depression (Spiritual Depression, 1965)
items.body:
Martyn Lloyd-Jones was a doctor before becoming one of the greatest preachers of the twentieth century, in London. In Spiritual Depression, he gathered sermons about Christian discouragement. The first of these comes from Psalm 42, where the psalmist asks: "Why are you downcast, O my soul? Wait in God."

## The secret of Psalm 42

Lloyd-Jones observes something that changes everything: the psalmist is not just listening to his own soul; he is speaking to it. Most of our unhappiness, says the preacher, comes from listening to ourselves instead of talking to ourselves. Yesterday's thoughts, tomorrow's fears, and the accusations of the heart speak nonstop, and we simply accept everything they say.

## Preach to oneself

The way out is to take the reins: interrupt the soul, ask why it is downcast, and remind it of who God is, what He has done, and what He promised. This is not forced optimism; it is applied faith. The psalmist does not deny the pain, but places it before the truth: "I will praise him still."

## Various causes

As a doctor, Lloyd-Jones recognizes that discouragement can have physical causes, temperament, fatigue, or difficult circumstances, and that these factors need to be handled wisely, including with professional help. But he also shows spiritual causes: looking more at oneself than at Christ, living under condemnation already removed, or expecting constant emotion from the Christian life.

## For your day

Try the psalmist's method. When anxiety speaks, respond with a promise from Scripture. Write it down, read it aloud, repeat it throughout the day. You are not required to believe everything your heart says; you are invited to tell your heart what God says.

items.title: Anxiety and the struggle against disbelief
items.author: John Piper
items.work: Future Grace (1995)
items.body:
John Piper wrote Future Grace to answer a practical question: how to fight sin and anxiety in a Christian way? His answer is that many of our sins are born from a common root: failing to trust in what God promised to do for us tomorrow.

## Past grace and future grace

Piper distinguishes the grace we have already received—the cross, forgiveness, and our conversion—from the grace God promises for the future: strength for today, provision for tomorrow, presence in every trial. Gratitude looks back. But, Piper says, the Christian life is lived mainly through faith that looks forward.

## Anxiety as a question of faith

For Piper, anxiety is not just an emotion; it is often a symptom of unbelief in God's promises. This should not become an accusation, but a hopeful diagnosis. If the root is unbelief, the remedy is faith. Jesus does exactly that in the Sermon on the Mount: when concerned with food and clothing, he points to the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies (Matthew 6:25–34).

## Struggling with promises

Piper's method is concrete: identify anxiety, choose a biblical promise that speaks directly to it, and struggle with that promise. Against fear of the future, Isaiah 41:10. Against lack, Philippians 4:19. Against guilt, Romans 8:1. He says he memorizes verses precisely to have them at hand in those moments.

## A necessary care

Not all anxiety is simply lack of faith; there are physical and emotional causes that call for care and, sometimes, treatment. Piper acknowledges this. But he insists that, in all situations, God's promise is a powerful remedy that should not be set aside. Future grace is the certainty that the God who gave us the Son will also give us all things.

items.title: When the preacher becomes discouraged
items.author: Charles H. Spurgeon
items.work: Lectures to My Students, lecture "The Minister's Fainting"
items.body:
Few people imagine that Charles Spurgeon, the preacher who filled temples in London, struggled with deep bouts of sadness for much of his life. He spoke about this openly to the students at his seminary in a lecture about the minister's "fainting." This honesty is a gift for every Christian facing discouragement.

## Even the strong fall

Spurgeon recalls that the great men of the Bible also became discouraged. Elijah asked to die under a bush (1 Kings 19). Jeremiah cursed the day he was born. David asked his own soul why it was downcast. If they went through this, we should not be surprised when it happens to us.

## Various causes

With wisdom, Spurgeon points out various causes: the fragile body, work fatigue, loneliness, criticism, losses, and even moments that come right after great victories. He himself suffered from gout and other illnesses, and recognized that body and soul are connected. That is why he recommends rest, fresh air, and care for health, without neglecting the common means God gives.

## Grace in the darkness

Spurgeon also saw spiritual purpose in his suffering. He wrote that crises made him humbler, more dependent on God, and more compassionate toward those who suffered. The dark valley taught what the illuminated pulpit did not.

## For those in the valley

If you are going through a time of sadness, Spurgeon would say: you are no less Christian because of it. Seek help, including professional help when needed, take care of your body, talk to trusted brothers, and keep leaning on Christ, even if it is with little strength. The same God who fed Elijah in the desert cares for you.

items.title: Walking with God amid pain
items.author: Tim Keller
items.work: Walking with God Amid Pain and Suffering (2013)
items.body:
Tim Keller wrote this book after years of accompanying people in mourning and after his own experience with cancer. He later faced pancreatic cancer, from which he died in 2023, publicly speaking of the hope for resurrection. The book addresses suffering from three angles: philosophical, biblical, and personal.

## Every culture needs to explain pain

Keller begins by showing that all cultures have a theory for suffering. Some say it is illusion, others that it is punishment, others that it is a lack of technique or money. Modern secular culture has little to offer, because if this life is everything, suffering can only be avoided or endured, never redeemed.

## The God who suffered

Christianity offers something unique: a God who entered into suffering. Keller says we do not know why God allows each specific pain, but we know it is not because He does not care, for He Himself suffered on the cross. The cross does not answer all questions, but it answers the most important one: God loves us.

## Walking through the furnace

Using the image from Daniel 3, in which a fourth man appears with the three young men in the furnace, Keller shows that God does not always deliver us from the fire, but promises to be with us in it. Suffering can refine faith, like gold is purified. And the Scriptures give words for this: to mourn, to pray honestly, to remember the promises.

## A path, not a technique

Keller observes that people suffer in different ways, and the Bible treats this with care: there is suffering from self-guilt, betrayal, loss, and mystery. There is no single formula. There is a Person to walk with. And there is hope: resurrection, when every tear will be wiped away and every loss restored.

items.title: Meaning in suffering: what Jordan Peterson sees, and what only the gospel gives
items.author: Jordan B. Peterson (com uma leitura reformada)
items.work: 12 Rules for Life (2018) and We Who Wrestle with God (2024)
items.body:
Jordan Peterson, a Canadian clinical psychologist, has become one of the most heard voices among young people in recent years. He is not a retired theologian and has never presented himself as such, but he often speaks about the Bible and suffering. Therefore, it is worth listening to him attentively and with discernment.

## What Peterson gets right

Peterson starts from a statement many avoid: life is marked by suffering. He refuses easy promises of happiness and says the path to a meaningful life is to take responsibility, tell the truth, and carry a heavy burden with courage. In 12 Rules for Life, advice like "tidy your room" and "tell the truth, or at least don't lie" echoes the wisdom of Proverbs. For a generation tired of victimhood, this sounds like liberation.

## Where to read it stops

Peterson reads biblical stories mainly as psychological maps and profound archetypes about the human condition. He treats the Bible with unusual seriousness, but often appears hesitant when directly asked if he believes in the historical resurrection of Jesus. A Reformed reading recognizes the value of what he observes, but reminds us that the Scriptures are not just symbols: they are the Word of God that narrates facts, culminating in Christ crucified and risen.

## Responsibility and grace

Here is the decisive difference. Peterson's path is to carry one's own cross as a heroic ideal. The gospel also calls for responsibility, but it begins elsewhere: Christ carried the cross that we could not carry. Without this, responsibility becomes overwhelming weight or pride. With that, it becomes gratitude. Suffering makes sense not because we are strong, but because God uses it to conform us to the image of the Son (Romans 8:28–29).

## How to talk to someone who listens to Peterson

Many young people come to church because of him. The suggestion is to start with what he gets right: truth, order, responsibility, seriousness with the Bible. And then take the step he does not take: present the real Christ, who is not only a model of courage but also the Savior of sinners and the risen Lord.

items.title: The broken cane
items.author: Richard Sibbes
items.work: The Bruised Reed (1630)
items.body:
Richard Sibbes was known in seventeenth-century England as "the sweet dispenser," for the tenderness with which he preached grace. His most famous book was born from sermons on Isaiah 42:3, quoted in Matthew 12:20: "He will not crush the broken reed, nor extinguish the smoldering wick."

## Who is the broken cane

Sibbes explains the images. Sugarcane is already a fragile plant; broken, it seems useless. The smoldering wick has almost no fire, only smoke. This is how many Christians are: wounded by guilt, weakened by suffering, with a faith that looks more like smoke than it calls. And it is precisely with these that Christ takes special care.

## The tenderness of Christ

Sibbes shows that Christ does not treat the weak harshly. He does not require perfect faith to begin helping. He blows the small ember until it lights up. One of the most remembered phrases in the book says, in short, that there is more mercy in Christ than sin in us. This does not lessen sin; it magnifies the Savior.

## The good side of the wound

Sibbes also sees purpose in fragility. God breaks to heal. The wound of repentance and the weight of trial empty us of self-sufficiency and make us run to Christ. A broken reed that leans on Christ is safer than a proud tree that leans on itself.

## A word for the tired

If your faith seems like smoke, Sibbes would say: do not extinguish the little you have with despair. Take the embers to Christ. He does not despise them. The broken cane does not need to feign strength; it only needs to be close to the one who is meek and humble in heart.

items.title: Why love the local church
items.author: Kevin DeYoung
items.work: Why We Love the Church (with Ted Kluck, 2009)
items.body:
Kevin DeYoung, a Presbyterian pastor in the United States, wrote with his friend Ted Kluck a book with a provocative title for a generation distrustful of institutions: Why We Love the Church. The book responds to Christians who say they love Jesus but don't want to know about the church.

## Jesus and His Bride

The central argument is biblical and simple: you cannot love Christ and despise what He loves. The New Testament calls the church the body of Christ, the temple of the Spirit, and the bride of the Lamb. Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it (Ephesians 5:25). A faith that calls itself Christian but lives disconnected from the community is disconnected from Christ Himself.

## The criticism, taken seriously

DeYoung does not hide the church's flaws: hypocrisy, conflicts, mediocre cults, failing leaders. But he reminds us that the church was never a community of the perfect; it has always been a hospital for sinners in treatment. Paul's letters were written to churches full of problems, and yet he calls them holy and beloved.

## The value of the common

One of the book's strongest points is the defense of ordinary faithfulness. Going to service every Sunday, listening to the sermon, attending the Supper, serving in dull tasks, living with different people. DeYoung says that this is how, slowly and almost invisibly, God forms mature Christians. The church doesn't have to be spectacular; it needs to be faithful.

## An honest question

If you have distanced yourself from the church because of real wounds, the book does not disregard them. But it invites you to take a step back, seeking a church that preaches the Word faithfully, administers the sacraments, and cares for people. Loving the church is, in the end, a way to love Christ the way He chose to be loved.

items.title: A service with Christ at the center
items.author: Michael Horton
items.work: Christianity without Christ? (Christless Christianity, 2008)
items.body:
Michael Horton, a Reformed theologian and professor at Westminster Seminary in California, made a harsh diagnosis of the contemporary church: many communities talk a lot about God, but almost nothing about Christ. The problem, he says, is not necessarily open heresy, but distraction. Christ is mentioned, but he is not the center.

## Therapeutic moralism

Horton uses an expression coined by sociologists to describe the faith of many young people: a moralistic and therapeutic deism. God exists, wants us to be good, and wants us to feel good. In this model, worship becomes a moment of motivation and preaching becomes a list of tips for life. The gospel, the news of what God did in Christ for sinners, disappears.

## Law and gospel

Following Luther and the Reformed tradition, Horton insists on distinguishing law and gospel. The law tells us what we must do; the gospel announces what God has made. The two are words of God, but they cannot be confused. A preaching of law alone crushes or exaggerates. A preaching that announces Christ crucified and risen nourishes faith and produces true fruit.

## God serves His people

Horton recalls a central idea of the Reformation: in worship, before we serve God, God serves us. He speaks by the preached Word, forgives us by absolution, feeds us by the Supper, and marks us by baptism. The means of grace are not empty rituals; they are the way Christ gives Himself to His church.

## For next Sunday

A useful question when leaving the service is: have I heard today what God has done in Christ, or only what I should do? Good preaching also applies and exhorts, but always from grace. A service with Christ at the center restores to each believer the joy of receiving, and only then the strength to obey.

items.title: What are they doing with the church?
items.author: Augustus Nicodemus Lopes
items.work: What They're Doing with the Church (2008)
items.body:
Augustus Nicodemus Lopes is a Presbyterian pastor and one of the best-known Reformed theologians in Brazil, with a long career in theological teaching. In 2008, he published a book that sparked debate by frankly analyzing the directions of the Brazilian evangelical movement. This article presents, in our own words, the central concerns of the work.

## Growth and crisis

The book acknowledges the impressive growth of evangelicals in Brazil, but asks: growth of what? For the author, numbers are not enough. A church can grow in frequency and decrease in biblical fidelity. Visible success alone is not a sign of blessing.

## Identified deviations

Among the concerns raised are prosperity theology, which turns God into a means to obtain goods; the abandonment of expository preaching in favor of motivational messages; the personalism of unaccountable leaders; and practices that place experiences above Scripture. The tone is one of pastoral warning, not contempt.

## The way back

The proposed answer is old: return to the Scriptures. Faithful preaching of the biblical text, worship centered on God, qualified leadership according to 1 Timothy 3, discipline with love, and a gospel that speaks of sin, cross, repentance, and faith. The sixteenth-century Reformation remains a model: the Reformed church must always be reforming itself by the Word.

## To reflect on

The question the book leaves applies to every local church and to every Christian: what has shaped our faith, the Bible, or the trends of the moment? Loving the church includes wanting it to be faithful to its Lord.

items.title: The Supper: Christ truly nourishes us
items.author: João Calvino
items.work: Small Treatise on the Last Supper (1541) and Institutes IV.17
items.body:
At the time of the Reformation, the Last Supper was one of the most debated topics. Catholics advocated transubstantiation. Lutherans affirmed the physical presence of Christ with the bread. Zwingli tended to see the Supper mainly as a memorial. Calvin sought a path faithful to the Scriptures that became the teaching of the Reformed confessions.

## Sign and reality

Calvin teaches that bread and wine are signs, but not empty signs. Just as the rainbow was a sign of the promise to Noah, the Last Supper is a sign and seal of Christ's promise. And God does not deceive: what He shows in the sign, He actually gives to the believer by faith.

## Real communion by the Spirit

The glorified body of Christ is in heaven, says Calvin. But, through the work of the Holy Spirit, we are lifted up to Him and truly nourished with His life. It is not about eating the physical flesh of Christ, nor just remembering a fact from the past. It is real communion with the living Christ. That is why the ancient Reformed liturgy invited the faithful: "lift up your hearts."

## Who is the Supper for

The Supper is not a reward for the perfect, but a remedy for the sick who trust in Christ. Calvin writes that no one should turn away because they feel unworthy, as long as they recognize their own sin, trust in Christ, and desire to live for Him. The examination Paul asks for in 1 Corinthians 11 is not a search for perfection, but for sincere repentance and faith.

## A practical suggestion

At the next Supper, try preparing your heart during the week: confessing sins, seeking reconciliation with those in conflict, and meditating on a passage about the cross. When eating and drinking, remember that it is not you who hold Christ; it is He who holds you.

items.title: Baptism: sign and seal of the covenant
items.author: Tradição reformada (Heidelberg e Westminster)
items.work: Heidelberg Catechism (1563), questions 69–74; Westminster Confession, chap. 28
items.body:
Baptism is the visible gateway to the church. In the Reformed tradition, it is understood from a concept that runs throughout the Bible: the covenant. God does not relate to His people vaguely, but through solemn promises, accompanied by visible signs.

## What baptism means

The Heidelberg Catechism teaches that the water of baptism points to the blood of Christ and to the Spirit, which cleanses the soul from all sins, just as water washes away the filth of the body. Baptism does not save by itself, as if water had magical power. It is a sign and seal: it shows and confirms the promise of the gospel.

## A mark of belonging

Just as circumcision marked the children of Abraham in the Old Testament, baptism marks those who belong to God's people. That is why Presbyterian and Reformed churches also baptize the children of believers, understanding that the promises are "for you and for your children" (Acts 2:39). Reformed Baptist churches, such as those following the 1689 Confession present in the SOLA, understand that baptism should be given to those who profess the faith. It is a real difference between brothers who agree on the gospel of grace.

## Living baptism

Luther said that, in times of temptation, he remembered: "I was baptized." The idea is that baptism is not just an event of the past; it is a reality to live every day. He reminds us that we belong to Christ, that we were buried with him for sin and raised to new life (Romans 6:3–4).

## For today

If you have already been baptized, the question is: am I living as someone who belongs to Christ? If not, the invitation is to talk to your church pastor about this step. In both cases, baptism points beyond itself: to God's faithful promise.

items.title: "I was baptized"
items.author: Martinho Lutero
items.work: Major Catechism (1529), part about baptism
items.body:
It is said that Martin Luther, in moments of greatest temptation and anguish, wrote or said to himself: "I was baptized." It was not superstition. It was a way to cling to God's promise when feelings failed. In his Major Catechism, written for pastors and families, he explains why baptism is a treasure for life.

## The Word by the Water

Luther teaches that baptism is not just water; it is water united to the Word and the command of God. What gives value to baptism is not the element, but the promise: "whoever believes and is baptized will be saved" (Mark 16:16). That is why he insists that baptism must be received with faith, and that faith rests on the promise, not on our experience.

## A baptism for every day

For Luther, baptism is not in the past. He describes the Christian life as a daily baptism: the old man is drowned by repentance and the new man rises by faith, every day. Romans 6 describes exactly that: buried with Christ, resurrected to walk in newness of life.

## Consolation in the accusations

When conscience accuses and the devil says "you do not belong to God," Luther responds with the objective fact: I was baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. God's promise is firmer than our feelings. The Reformed and Baptist traditions diverge from Luther on points about the sacraments, but all can learn from this consolation: the believer relies on God's promise, not on himself.

## For today

The next time you witness a baptism in your church, remember yours. Ask: am I living as someone who was buried and resurrected with Christ? The visible sign points to the invisible reality: you belong to it.

items.title: Rejoice, the peoples
items.author: John Piper
items.work: Let the Nations Be Glad! (Let the Nations Be Glad!, 1993)
items.body:
John Piper's book on missions begins with one of the most quoted phrases in contemporary missiology: missions exist because worship does not exist. The ultimate goal of the church, Piper says, is not missions, but worship. Missions are the means; the worship of God among all peoples is the end.

## God's passion for His glory

Piper shows that, throughout the Bible, God acts so that His name is known and praised in all nations. This is not vanity, but love, because the greatest good for anyone is to know and enjoy God. When God seeks His glory, He seeks our joy.

## Peoples, not just countries

An important chapter deals with the concept of peoples in the Bible. The Great Commission commands disciples from "all nations" (Matthew 28:19), and the Greek word refers to ethnic and cultural groups, not just political borders. There are still thousands of peoples with little or no presence of the gospel. The task is not finished.

## Supremacy of Christ

Piper also faces a difficult question: can someone who has never heard of Jesus be saved by another way? He argues, based on texts like Acts 4:12 and Romans 10:14–15, that conscious faith in Christ is necessary for salvation. That is why missions are urgent. It is not about pressure, but about love for real people and for a unique Savior.

## Go, send, or pray

Piper often says that Christians have three options when it comes to missions: go, send, or disobey. Not everyone is called to cross the sea, but everyone can pray, offer, welcome missionaries, and reach the nations already living in their city. The question is: what is your place in this work?

items.title: Evangelization and the sovereignty of God
items.author: J. I. Packer
items.work: Evangelism and the Sovereignty of God (Evangelism and the Sovereignty of God, 1961)
items.body:
Many Christians think they need to choose: either God is sovereign in salvation, and then evangelizing seems unnecessary; or evangelization is urgent, and then God's sovereignty seems an obstacle. J. I. Packer wrote this little book to show that this choice is false.

## An antinomy, not a contradiction

Packer uses the word antinomy: two truths that seem out of place, but are both taught by the Bible. God is sovereign and chooses who will be saved. And the human being is responsible and must heed the call to repentance and faith. The Bible teaches both things without embarrassment, and we must believe in both, even without fully understanding how they relate.

## What evangelizing means

Packer defines evangelism carefully: it is proclaiming the message of Christ and calling people to repent and believe. It is not manipulating emotions or measuring success by decisions. Evangelizing is being faithful in communicating the gospel; converting is God's work.

## The sovereignty that encourages

Far from cooling evangelism, says Packer, God's sovereignty is our greatest hope. If conversion depended on our skill, no one would be saved, because dead hearts do not respond to arguments. But God opens hearts, as He opened Lydia's (Acts 16:14). That is why we can speak boldly and patiently, without despair and without tricks.

## To practice

The book ends with an appeal: pray for people, truly love them, and speak of Christ clearly. Trust that God uses the faithfully proclaimed message. The result is in His hands; faithfulness, in ours.

items.title: The Soul Winner
items.author: Charles H. Spurgeon
items.work: The Soul Winner (1895)
items.body:
Charles Spurgeon was a committed Calvinist and, at the same time, one of the most passionate evangelists in history. For him, believing in God's sovereignty was never a reason to fold his arms. The book The Soul Winner gathers lectures given to students and sermons on the subject, based on Proverbs 11:30: "He who wins souls is wise."

## What does it mean to win souls

Spurgeon makes it clear that winning souls is not about increasing the number of members or making hasty decisions. It is about seeing truly converted people: repentant, believing in Christ, and changed. He warned against methods that produce numbers but not disciples.

## The qualities of the winner

Spurgeon points out spiritual qualities: holiness of life, because the inconsistent preacher drives people away; serious knowledge of the Word; humility; and, above all, true love for people. He said that one must have a broken heart for the lost. He who does not weep for souls will hardly reach them.

## How to speak of Christ

The practical advice is many: speak clearly, without jargon; be direct but kind; use the Scriptures; respond to objections patiently; and call to decision, inviting trust in Christ now. Spurgeon also emphasizes the role of every church member, not just pastors: a word at home, at work, or in a letter can be used by God.

## Prayer and dependence

The book ends where it all begins: in prayer. Only the Holy Spirit converts, says Spurgeon. That is why the soul winner plants and waters on his knees. The question for us is simple: for whom are you praying, by name, so that it may come to Christ?

items.title: Take God seriously in His Word
items.author: Kevin DeYoung
items.work: Taking God at His Word (2014)
items.body:
Kevin DeYoung wrote a short and accessible book about the doctrine of the Scriptures. The aim is to help ordinary Christians understand why to trust the Bible, and how to love it. He organizes the doctrine into four words that form an English acronym: sufficient, clear, final, and necessary.

## Enough

The Bible contains everything we need to know for salvation and to live in a way pleasing to God (2 Timothy 3:16–17). This does not mean it answers all the technical questions of life, but that nothing essential for faith and obedience is missing. We do not need new revelations to know God's will.

## Clara

DeYoung advocates for the clarity of Scripture: what is necessary for salvation is laid out in a way that anyone, with ordinary means, can understand. There are difficult passages, of course. But the Bible is not a secret book for experts. It was written to be read at home, in church, and in everyday life.

## Final

The Bible is the final authority. Traditions, experiences, feelings, and opinions of experts have their place, but they must be judged by the Word, not the other way around. This was the principle of the Reformation known as Sola Scriptura, which gives its name to SOLA itself.

## Required

Without God's revelation, we would not know the gospel. Creation shows that God exists, but only Scripture shows how sinners can be reconciled to Him. That is why DeYoung ends with an affectionate appeal: the entire Psalm 119 is a declaration of love for the Word. He asks the reader if he can say the same: "How much I love your law!"

items.title: God spoke: the reliability of the Bible
items.author: J. I. Packer
items.work: Fundamentalism and the Word of God (1958) and the Chicago Declaration on Inerrancy (1978)
items.body:
J. I. Packer dedicated much of his life to defending the authority of the Scriptures. While still young, he wrote a book responding to criticisms accusing evangelicals of obscurantism. Later, he was one of the signatories and drafters of the Chicago Declaration on Biblical Inerrancy, a document that still guides many churches today.

## The Word of God in human words

Packer insists that the Bible is entirely human word and entirely the Word of God. The authors wrote with their styles, contexts, and personalities. But the Holy Spirit led them in such a way that what they wrote is exactly what God meant (2 Peter 1:21). Inspiration does not nullify the human; it guarantees the divine.

## Why inerrancy matters

For Packer, inerrancy is not an isolated technical thesis, but a consequence of God's character. If God does not lie, His Word is true in everything it affirms. This does not mean reading the Bible mechanically: it is necessary to respect literary genres, figurative language, and the purpose of each text. But it means rejecting the idea that we can choose which parts are reliable.

## Jesus and the Scriptures

Packer's strongest argument is Christological: Jesus treated the Old Testament as the Word of God that cannot fail (John 10:35). If we are disciples of Christ, we must receive the Scriptures as He received them. Our view of the Bible is, at its core, a matter of following the Master.

## A doctrine to live by

Packer warned that it is possible to defend inerrancy and not obey the Bible. That is why doctrine must always end in practice: reading, meditating, believing, and obeying. The Bible is reliable so that we can rest in it and live for it.

items.title: How to Read the Bible: Lessons from the History of Interpretation
items.author: Augustus Nicodemus Lopes
items.work: The Bible and Its Interpreters (2004)
items.body:
In The Bible and Its Interpreters, Augustus Nicodemus Lopes traces the history of how the Bible was read over the centuries, from Jewish rabbis and the Church Fathers to the Reformation and the historical-critical method. The goal is not only to inform, but to help today's reader interpret the Scriptures well. This article summarizes, in our own words, the main lessons.

## The dangers of allegory

One of the lessons of history is the risk of uncontrolled allegory. For centuries, many interpreters sought hidden meanings in every detail of the text, and thus could make the Bible say almost anything. The text ceased to correct the reader and began to reflect the ideas of the reader.

## The turning point of the Reformation

Reformers, like Luther and Calvin, insisted on seeking the natural meaning of the text, considering grammar, historical context, and the author's intention. This path became known as the grammatical-historical method. And they added a precious principle: Scripture interprets Scripture. Clearer passages illuminate the more difficult ones.

## The modern challenge

The book also evaluates modern historical criticism, which often treats the Bible only as human literature, distrusting miracles and inspiration. The Reformed response is not to ignore historical questions, but to investigate them believing that Scripture is the Word of God.

## For the average reader

Some simple questions help anyone: what does the text say? What did it mean for early readers? How does it fit into the entire Bible and point to Christ? And what does God call me to believe and do? Reading the Bible well is a way to love God with understanding.

items.title: Delighting in the Trinity
items.author: Michael Reeves
items.work: Delighting in the Trinity (Delighting in the Trinity, 2012)
items.body:
Michael Reeves, a British theologian, wrote a book with a bold proposal: to show that the Trinity is not a mathematical puzzle for theologians, but the heart of the Christian faith and the source of our joy. For him, who God is determines everything, including how we live.

## Before creation, there was love

Reeves starts from John 17:24, when Jesus speaks of the love the Father had for Him before the foundation of the world. Before any creature existed, God was already love: the Father loving the Son in the Spirit. A solitary god would need to create the world to have someone to love. The triune God creates not out of necessity, but out of overflow of love.

## A God who gives Himself

In creation, the Father does all things through the Son and by the power of the Spirit. In salvation, the Father sends the Son, who gives Himself for us, and the Spirit unites us to Him. Reeves shows that salvation is being brought into this love that already existed. We are adopted to enjoy, as children, the fellowship that the Son has had with the Father since always.

## A Trinitarian life

This changes the Christian life. Prayer is speaking with the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. Holiness is resembling the God who is love, and not just following rules. The mission of the church is the overflow of the same love that led the Father to send the Son. Even our joy in God is a gift of the Spirit, who pours that love into our hearts (Romans 5:5).

## For meditation

Reeves suggests a question: when you think of God, do you first think of a supreme power or of a Father who loves the Son? The answer shapes everything. The book's invitation is simple: to know the triune God and delight in Him.

items.title: Augustine and the restless heart
items.author: Agostinho de Hipona
items.work: Confessions (c. 400) and The Trinity (c. 400–420)
items.body:
Augustine, bishop of Hippo in North Africa, is one of the Church Fathers most cited by reformers. Calvin mentions him hundreds of times in the Institutes. Two of his works show how the doctrine of God touches life: the Confessions, a long autobiographical prayer, and The Trinity, a profound treatise on the triune God.

## Made for God

The Confessions begin with a phrase that has spanned the centuries: "You made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you." Augustine tells his own story of seeking pleasure, success, and wisdom, and concludes that none of this satisfies us, because we were created for something greater. Human restlessness is, at its core, longing for God.

## The love that is God

In The Trinity, Augustine seeks to understand, with reverence, how God is one and three. He starts from 1 John 4:8, "God is love," and observes that love presupposes someone who loves, someone who is loved, and the love itself that unites them. He himself acknowledges that no image is perfect, but reflection helps to see that the Trinity is not a cold enigma: it is the eternal communion of love of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit.

## Know to love

For Augustine, studying God is not just an intellectual exercise. The goal is to love more the one we know. He says that our soul is like an image of God stained by sin, and that grace restores it as we contemplate God in Christ. Theology and worship walk together.

## For today

Augustine's question applies: where has your heart sought rest? Work, approval, comfort, and entertainment promise peace, but do not sustain. The rest we seek has a name: the triune God who revealed Himself in Jesus Christ and invites us to return home.

items.title: The Trinity, heart of faith
items.author: Herman Bavinck
items.work: Reformed Dogmatics, vol. 2 (Gereformeerde Dogmatiek, 1895–1901)
items.body:
In his great Reformed Dogmatics, Herman Bavinck devoted extensive pages to the doctrine of God. He reached a conclusion that marks all his theology: the Trinity is not an appendix of the Christian faith, but its living center. In his words, in summary, it is in the triune God that beats the heart of all revelation.

## Without the Trinity, another gospel

Bavinck observes that all the great truths of faith depend on the Trinity. Creation is the work of the Father through the Son in the Spirit. Redemption is the Father sending the Son and the Spirit applying the work of the Son. If we remove the Trinity, the incarnation loses meaning, the cross loses value, and the indwelling of the Spirit becomes mere influence. Therefore, Bavinck says, the great errors in church history almost always began with deviations in God's doctrine.

## Mystery that feeds

Bavinck is reverent. He states that the Trinity is a mystery that we cannot master with reason, but that we can know because God revealed Himself. It is not contradiction, because God is not one and three in the same sense: He is one in essence and three in persons. Theology, for Bavinck, begins and ends in worship.

## The God who relates

One of Bavinck's most beautiful contributions is to show that God is not eternal solitude. In Him there is life, communion, and love from the beginning. That is why creation was not a necessity of God, but an overflow of His fullness. And that is why salvation is being included in this divine life as children.

## For life

Trinitarian faith changes the way we pray and live. We pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. We are called to live in communion, reflecting the God who is communion. And we await the day when we will see face to face the triune God, source of all joy.

items.title: Meek and humble: the heart of Christ
items.author: Dane Ortlund
items.work: Gentle and Lowly (2020)
items.body:
Dane Ortlund wrote a book that surprised with its scope: a study on the heart of Christ that touched readers worldwide. The starting point is Matthew 11:29, the only place in the Gospels where Jesus describes His own heart: "I am meek and humble in heart."

## Who Jesus is inside

Ortlund notes that Jesus could have described himself in many ways: holy, powerful, just. And he is all of that. But when he opens his own heart, he says: meek and humble. It's not that Jesus doesn't have anger against sin; it's that his heart naturally leans toward the weary, the overwhelmed, and sinners.

## The Puritans Rediscovered

The book dialogues extensively with the Puritans, especially Thomas Goodwin and Richard Sibbes. Goodwin wrote about the heart of Christ in heaven, showing that the ascension did not cool Jesus' love. Sibbes, in The Broken Reed, explores Isaiah 42:3: he does not crush the broken reed nor extinguish the smoldering wick. Ortlund brings these ancient works to today's reader.

## For those who fall again

The strongest application is for the Christian who stumbles repeatedly. Many imagine that Jesus grows tired of them, that there is a limit to divine patience. Ortlund shows the opposite: the believer's sin provokes in Christ not repulsion, but compassion. He not only forgives; he draws near. This does not diminish the seriousness of the sin; it increases the beauty of grace.

## An invitation

Matthew 11 ends with an invitation: "Come to me... and you will find rest." Ortlund asks the reader: how do you imagine Jesus looking at you at this moment? If the answer is disappointment, maybe it's time to let Jesus Himself correct that image.

items.title: True God and true man
items.author: Anselmo de Cantuária e o Concílio de Calcedônia
items.work: Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo, 1098) and Definition of Chalcedon (451)
items.body:
Why did God become man? The question gives its title to a work by Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury in the eleventh century, and touches on the heart of the Christian faith. Centuries earlier, the Council of Chalcedon had precisely formulated who Jesus is. Together, Anselm and Chalcedon help to understand why the person of Christ matters so much.

## The definition of Chalcedon

In 451, the bishops gathered in Chalcedon affirmed that Jesus Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation. These four denials protect the mystery: Jesus is not half God and half man, nor a special man adopted by God, nor God pretending to be man. He is fully God and fully man. The Definition of Chalcedon is in SOLA, in the creeds section.

## Anselmo's argument

Anselm reasons thus: sin is an offense against the infinite honor of God, and humanity owes a satisfaction it cannot pay. Only God could pay, but only man should pay. Therefore, someone who was both God and man was necessary. The incarnation was not a detail; it was the only adequate response to the problem of sin. The reformers deepened this idea when speaking of penal substitution: Christ received in our place the punishment we deserved.

## Why it matters

If Jesus were not God, His death would not have infinite value. If He were not man, He could neither represent us nor have compassion for our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). Chalcedon and Anselm protect the same truth: our Savior is sufficient to save and close to comfort.

## For meditation

Next time you read the Gospels, notice both sides: Jesus tired, hungry, crying; and Jesus calming the storm, forgiving sins, raising the dead. It is the same person. And it is this person who intercedes for us today.

items.title: The Heart of Christ in Heaven
items.author: Thomas Goodwin
items.work: The Heart of Christ in Heaven with Sinners on Earth (1651)
items.body:
Thomas Goodwin, an English Puritan and one of the theologians of the Westminster Assembly, wrote a work with a long title and a simple question: after Jesus ascended to heaven and was glorified, does His heart remain the same with sinners? Or did glory make Him distant?

## The same Jesus

Goodwin answers firmly: the same. The Jesus who wept with Martha and Mary, who touched lepers and received sinners, is the Jesus who today is at the right hand of the Father. The ascension did not harden his heart. On the contrary, he remains human, with glorified human affections, and therefore sympathizes with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

## The last words before leaving

Goodwin analyzes Jesus' speeches in John 13 to 17, given on the eve of the cross. There Jesus promises not to leave the disciples orphaned, prepares a place for them, and prays for them. Goodwin sees in these words a window into what Jesus feels now. If he loved like that before going, he loves like that after arriving.

## Growing compassion

A bold point from the book: Goodwin suggests that glory increased Christ's capacity to love, rather than diminishing it. He is freer and fuller to have compassion on His own. When a believer suffers or sins, Christ's heart moves toward him, to rescue and restore.

## For those who feel far away

Dane Ortlund popularized this work in Meek and Humble, also in SOLA. Goodwin invites us to replace the image of a distant Christ with an intercessor Christ, who knows our name and bows down to us. Even today, he is praying for his own.
